name: Fair Lending and Bias Testing
title: Fair Lending and Bias Testing
answer: Fair lending and bias testing covers the review of credit decisions, pricing, underwriting and marketing for unlawful disparities by race, sex, age, national origin and other protected classes. It sits inside model risk management and compliance, and it draws on the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, the Fair Housing Act and the disparate impact standard rather than on any single technical method. The work applies to banks, credit unions, fintech lenders, mortgage servicers and the vendors that supply scoring and decisioning software to them.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Fair lending and bias testing covers the review of credit decisions, pricing, underwriting and marketing for unlawful disparities by race, sex, age, national origin and other protected classes. It sits inside model risk management and compliance, and it draws on the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, the Fair Housing Act and the disparate impact standard rather than on any single technical method. The work applies to banks, credit unions, fintech lenders, mortgage servicers and the vendors that supply scoring and decisioning software to them.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The practice runs on the lender's own loan application and servicing data, joined to geocoded census and HMDA-style public records that supply proxy variables where protected class is not collected. Teams work in a statistical environment such as R, Python or SAS, with model documentation and version history kept in a governed repository. Findings are usually reported through the same committee structure that handles model validation, with legal counsel and the fair lending officer reviewing results before anything is finalized.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts compare approval rates, pricing and exception rates across groups, then run regression or matched-pair analysis that holds creditworthiness constant so that a gap can be attributed to a protected characteristic rather than to risk. Proxy methods such as Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding are used to estimate race and ethnicity where the data is incomplete, and the results are checked against the lender's own fair lending history. Testing is repeated when a model is retrained, when a threshold changes, or when a new data source is added, because a disparity can appear without any change to the model itself.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The governing obligations come from the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, the Fair Housing Act, the Community Reinvestment Act and state-level fair lending statutes, enforced by agencies including the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Department of Justice. Documentation has to show what was tested, on which population, with which method, and what was done about any disparity found, since examiners and plaintiffs both read the record. Adverse action notices, model cards and vendor contracts are part of the same file, and a lender remains accountable for a disparity produced by a third-party score even when it did not build the model.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Supervisory attention is moving toward continuous monitoring rather than an annual review, with disparity metrics tracked alongside model performance in production. Lenders are also being asked to explain automated decisions in plain terms to applicants and to show that alternative data sources such as cash flow records do not introduce new gaps. The open questions are how to test generative and large language models used in servicing and collections, and how to keep a defensible record when the underlying model changes faster than the review cycle.
